title: IELTS vs Duolingo vs TOEFL: which test universities accept in 2027
summary: Universities set their own accepted tests and minimums, so compare the programme page, check the UK visa list separately, and pick the test that covers most of your list.

sources.title: UK government: student visa, English requirement

review_note: Verified on fetched official pages: gov.uk/student-visa (English requirement, eligibility, processing times). The IELTS, Duolingo and ETS citations are homepage-level and were not opened at check time (the IELTS partner page returned 404). The article gives no minimum scores or validity periods because none were verified; the reader is told to check each programme page. The UK visa test list was not opened (gov.uk page returned 404), so the article only states that it differs from university lists and must be checked on gov.uk.
body:
## In short

- There is no single "accepted" test for all universities. Each university or programme sets its own list of accepted tests and its own minimum scores.
- IELTS, TOEFL iBT and the Duolingo English Test are the three tests most students from Central Asia ask about. They measure similar skills, but the formats and score scales differ.
- For a UK student visa, the government has its own list of accepted tests. That list is not the same as a university's list, so check both.
- Read the programme page for the exact test name, minimum overall score, section minimums and how long the result is valid.

## What the three tests measure

**IELTS** is run by IELTS partners and is offered in paper and computer formats. It has four sections: listening, reading, writing and speaking. The speaking section is a face-to-face or video interview with an examiner.

**TOEFL iBT** is run by ETS. It is taken on a computer and tests reading, listening, speaking and writing, with the speaking and writing responses scored by a mix of human and automated methods.

**Duolingo English Test** is taken online, usually at home with a webcam, and includes adaptive questions. Its format is shorter and it is often cheaper, which is why many students consider it. Some universities accept it widely, but not all do, and some have specific rules for it.

Read each official site for the current format and fee. These details change, and blog summaries from earlier years often contain old figures.

## How universities decide

Admissions offices set minimum scores that can differ for each degree. A university might accept any of the three tests for one programme but only IELTS or TOEFL for another. Some universities ask for a minimum in every section, not only an overall score. A few accept a school-based English track or a previous English-medium education in place of a test.

Your job is to find the exact requirement for each programme on your list. Write down:

- The accepted tests, including any that are not accepted.
- The overall minimum and any section minimum.
- Whether a "superscore" or best-of-several-attempts policy applies.
- The validity period of the result. Results expire, and the period is set by the test provider and the university.
- Whether a result must be sent directly from the test provider.

## The UK visa question

If you plan to study in the UK, the student visa has its own English requirement. Gov.uk explains that you must be able to speak, read, write and understand English, and it refers to a separate page for the evidence. The tests the government accepts for visa purposes are not the same as the tests every university accepts. Some students pass a university's test but do not have a visa-approved result, or the reverse.

Before you book a test, check the gov.uk list of accepted tests, then check the university's programme page. If the two lists differ, the visa list is the one that matters for your visa application.

## Which test to choose

Choose based on the programmes you are targeting, not on price alone. A simple method:

1. List your target universities and programmes.
2. Note the accepted tests for each one.
3. Find the test that appears on the most lists.
4. Compare the total cost, including retakes, travel to a test centre and delivery time.
5. Book the earliest date that leaves room for a retake.

If one test is accepted by all your programmes, it is usually the simplest choice. If your programmes accept different tests, you may need to take two, so budget for that.

## Preparation timeline

Most students benefit from six to twelve weeks of focused practice, but the right length depends on your starting level. Use official practice materials where possible, because they match the real format. Practise speaking and writing with a teacher or a study partner, and track your section scores rather than only the overall number.

A realistic plan for 2027 entry:

- Early in the year before entry: find out your target tests and minimum scores.
- Spring: take a diagnostic test and decide on a study plan.
- Summer: sit your first attempt, leaving time for a second.
- Autumn: send official scores with your applications, and check each university's deadline for receiving them.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming a test accepted by one university is accepted everywhere.
- Using an old minimum score from a forum post.
- Sending a practice result or a screenshot instead of an official score report.
- Taking the test too late for the application deadline.
- Forgetting that the speaking section may need a separate booking.

## How to read a score report

A score report usually shows an overall score and a score for each section. Read them separately. Many programmes set a minimum for each section, so a high overall score can still fail if one section is low. Writing and speaking are the sections that most often hold students back, because they need practice with the format and the scoring criteria.

Check the validity date on the report. Some universities accept results only if they are recent, and the window is set by the university or the test provider. If your intended start date is far away, a result you take early may expire before you arrive.

## Practice that works

Use official practice tests where you can, because they follow the real format. Time yourself, and sit a full mock exam under test conditions at least twice before the real test. For speaking and writing, get feedback from a trained teacher, and keep a record of the errors that repeat. Errors in grammar, articles and word choice are common across all three tests, so a short daily routine often helps more than a long weekend session.

## Test day and technology

For online tests, check your internet connection, webcam, microphone and room setup a week before the exam. Read the provider's rules about what is allowed in the room. For centre-based tests, plan the journey and bring the identity document named in your booking. A small problem on test day can cost a full attempt and the fee, so check the details twice.

## What to do if your score is low

Do not panic. Look at the section that held you back, then decide whether a targeted practice plan is enough or whether a longer course is needed. Ask each university whether it accepts a retake and whether it uses the best score across several attempts. Some do, and some use the most recent result only. Confirm the policy on the official page before you book the next attempt.

## Checklist

- [ ] List the accepted tests for each target programme on its official page.
- [ ] Note overall and section minimums, and whether they differ by programme.
- [ ] Check the gov.uk accepted test list if you plan to apply for a UK visa.
- [ ] Choose one test that covers the most programmes on your list.
- [ ] Book a first attempt with time for a retake before the deadline.
- [ ] Confirm the validity period of your result against your intended start date.
- [ ] Ask each university how it wants scores sent, and when.
